chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 131 to 140, Ammoovanar's neythal decade spoken to the bard (பாணற்கு உரைத்த பத்து): the woman (once the man, once turning to the lord himself) uses the hero's bard as the ear for gossip, wasted shoulders and slipped bangles, rebukes him for carrying words instead of the man, and twice bids him look (காண்மதி பாண), once at beauty returned and once at bangles gone.

131.reading: The woman tells the bard that the friendship of the shore lord is good indeed, so long as no loud gossip rises in this town hedged with thillai.
131.nuance: The praise is hedged by its last line: the bond is good only at a time (காலே) when the town is quiet, so the opening நன்றே turns into a complaint that it cannot survive being known. The thillai hedge makes the town an enclosure that hears everything.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore lord (கொண்கன்) and the thillai hedge of the coastal town fix the seashore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem, which the decade title says is spoken to the bard: the gossip (கௌவை) of a secret bond points to kalavu; the friend could equally be the speaker

132.reading: The woman tells the bard that this town of the seashore grove, thick with punnai buds, has turned the very way the man shows her grace into gossip.
132.nuance: What the town talks about is not his neglect but his kindness (அருளும் ஆறே): his visits are the scandal. The punnai is only in bud (அரும்புமலி), and the gossip already blooms (அலர் also means a blossom).

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai of the seashore grove fixes the coast

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem, which the decade title says is spoken to the bard: the town's gossip about his favour points to kalavu

133.reading: The woman asks the bard what she can do, now that the lord of the gentle shore has left and her shoulders with their twisted bangles have grown dull without end.
133.nuance: புலம்பன், the shore lord's title, also means the lonely one; the word that names him names her state.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of the lonely shore (புலம்பன்) is the neythal hero's own name

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem, which the decade title says is spoken to the bard: என் புரிவளைத் தோளே shows the woman speaking of her own body

134.reading: The woman tells the bard to look: her dark-gold beauty has come back of its own accord together with the shore lord of the tall chariot whose leaping horses cross the wide backwater.
134.nuance: The beauty is the subject of the verb (தான் வந்தன்று): it returns by itself, riding in with him, as if it had left in his chariot. காண்மதி makes the bard a witness to the cure as he is elsewhere a witness to the wasting.

thinai_evidence.note: the wide backwater the chariot crosses fixes the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem, which the decade title says is spoken to the bard: என் மாமைக் கவினே shows the woman speaking of her own beauty on his return

135.reading: The speaker tells the bard that we are not sorrowful, if only we may win the consent of her with bamboo-round shoulders, a broad finely shaped waist and a chaplet of neythal flowers.
135.nuance: நேர்தல் may be her consent or a meeting; who speaks, and whether this is the man in kalavu or the friend vouching for the woman, the poem does not fix. Line 2 recurs as line 3 of Ainkurunuru 176.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal chaplet is the shore's own flower

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem, which the decade title says is spoken to the bard: the woman is described from outside (பணைத்தோள், அல்குல், கண்ணியை), so the man seems to speak; the friend speaking of the woman is also possible

136.reading: The woman tells the bard that he truly has no shame, pouring out words for the lord of the seashore ford who has made her bright, beautifully curved bangles slip.
136.nuance: சொல் உகுப்போய், 'you who spill words', makes the bard's eloquence a waste, set against what the lord's absence has spilled: the bangle off her wrist.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of the seashore ford fixes the coast

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem, which the decade title says is spoken to the bard: the bard pleading for the lord as go-between (வாயில்) suggests karpu

137.reading: The woman asks the bard one thing: do the women who desired the strong-chariot shore lord of his town ever get back their former beauty?
137.nuance: The plural நயந்தோர் counts her among many women who loved him, so the question is also a charge that he has made a habit of it. நும்மூர், 'your town', puts the bard on the lord's side.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore lord (கொண்கன்) is the neythal hero

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem, which the decade title says is spoken to the bard: the woman asks about the fate of those who loved him, herself among them

138.reading: The woman tells the bard that he truly has no decency: he has spoken loveless, harsh words in this town and has not brought back the lord of the gentle shore.
138.nuance: Whether the harsh words are the bard's own scolding of her people or the excuses he carries for the lord is not fixed by கழறி; either way he is blamed for bringing words instead of the man.

thinai_evidence.note: the soft land of the shore lord fixes the coast

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem, which the decade title says is spoken to the bard

139.reading: The woman tells the shore lord that more than he, who beguiles her fine beauty, it is his bard who ruins the beauty of good women.
139.nuance: The only poem of the decade not spoken to the bard: it turns to the lord and blames the bard, so that the man is let off lightly in words while the charge stands.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore lord (கொண்க) is the neythal hero

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem, which the decade title says is spoken to the bard: here the lord himself is addressed (கொண்க) and the bard spoken of, as the go-between who leads him to other women

140.reading: The woman tells the bard to look, for he is the one fit to tell it: the state in which her bright bangles, with their shining wrist-band, have left her since the lord of the ford went away.
140.nuance: The bard, rebuked in the decade for carrying the lord's words, is here asked to carry hers, and the message is not a speech but what he has seen. The decade closes on the same காண்மதி பாண as 134, with the opposite sight.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore lord of the ford fixes the coast

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem, which the decade title says is spoken to the bard

links.note: In Ainkurunuru 131 the woman says the lord's friendship is good only while no gossip rises in the town; in Kural 1147 the woman says the town's gossip is the manure on which her love-sickness grows.
links.teaches: Valluvar's woman turns the gossip into nourishment for her love, while the Sangam woman, speaking to the man's bard, treats the same gossip as the limit the bond cannot outlive, so the couplet's paradox rewrites a fear the older poem left plain.

links.note: 131 makes the friendship good only so long as gossip does not rise; 132 says the town has now made gossip of the lord's very grace.
links.teaches: Read in sequence the decade's first two poems pass from the condition to its breach: the gossip that 131 named as the bond's limit has arisen in 132, and it has risen not from his neglect but from his kindness.

links.note: Both have the woman's bangled shoulders lose their beauty when her partner leaves (Kural: துணைநீங்கித் தொல்கவின் வாடிய தோள்; Ainkurunuru: பிரிந்தெனப் புல்லென்றன என் புரிவளைத் தோளே).
links.teaches: The couplet describes the wasted shoulders as a fact, while the poem puts them as a helpless question to the absent man's own bard, so the same bodily sign becomes in the older poem a complaint lodged with his side of the household.

links.note: In Kural 1265 the woman wishes to see her husband (கொண்கனை) and says the pallor of her shoulders will then leave; in Ainkurunuru 134 she tells the bard her dark-gold beauty has come back with the chariot of the shore lord (கொண்க).
links.teaches: Valluvar states as a wish that only the sight of the husband will cure the pallor; the Sangam poem shows the cure already happened, the beauty arriving in his chariot, so the couplet's claim that news is not enough rests on the older scene of the bodily return.

links.note: 134 says the woman's beauty came back by itself with the shore lord; 137 asks whether the women who loved the lord ever get back their former beauty, implying they do not.
links.teaches: Within one decade the same speaker holds both that beauty returns with the lord and that those who loved him never regain it, so the decade shows the restored beauty of 134 as one turn of a cycle that 137 suspects will not last.

links.note: Both refuse the bard who comes with the shore lord's words: Natrinai 167 says his humble words will not remove the pallor of the bangled girl, Ainkurunuru 136 calls him shameless for pouring out words for the lord who made her bangles slip.
links.teaches: The Natrinai friend grants the bard's skill and denies only its effect, while the Ainkurunuru woman denies him decency itself, so set together they show the refusal of the go-between ranging from courtesy to contempt within the same neythal situation.

links.note: 136 (நாணிலை மன்ற பாண) blames the bard for spilling words for the lord; 138 (பண்பிலை மன்ற பாண) blames him for harsh words in the town and for not bringing the lord.
links.teaches: The paired rebukes show the bard condemned from both sides, for speaking on the lord's behalf and for failing to deliver the lord, so what the woman rejects is his offering words where only the man's presence would do.

links.note: In Akananuru 146 the wife, refusing the bard, says the woman who trusts the deceiving philanderer's word (மாயப் பரத்தன் வாய்மொழி) will lose her beauty; in Ainkurunuru 139 she tells the lord that his bard ruins good women's beauty more than he does.
links.teaches: The longer poem lays the ruin of beauty on the husband's own lying word, the short one shifts it to the bard who carries that word, so the pair shows the go-between counted as an agent of the harm and not merely its messenger.

links.note: In both the bard who came for the shore lord is told to report what he has seen of the woman: Natrinai 291 கண்டாங்கு உரையாய், Ainkurunuru 140 காண்மதி பாண நீ உரைத்தற்கு உரியை.
links.teaches: Ainkurunuru 140 names the message only as the state of her slipped bangles, while Natrinai 291 fills the same eyewitness report with a puram image of cattle raided at night, so the pair shows the three-line convention of the bard as witness expanded by borrowing from war poetry.

links.note: In Kural 1157 the woman says her slipping bangles spread the news that the shore lord (துறைவன்) has left her; in Ainkurunuru 140 she asks the bard to tell the lord of the ford (துறைகெழு கொண்கன்) the state of her bangles since he left.
links.teaches: Valluvar makes the bangles themselves the gossips who publish his departure, while the Sangam woman needs the bard to carry that sign to the man, so the couplet's bangles that speak for themselves compress a scene in which the body's testimony still had to be delivered.

source_issues: 131-140: the colophon gives no thurai for the decade (பாணற்கு உரைத்த பத்து), so every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem and the decade title.
139: the poem stands in two lines, the first unusually long (அம்ம வாழி கொண்க ... நின்னினும்); the line division looks like an e-text join, and the anthology's poems have 3 to 6 lines.
140: line 3 reads விறைகேழ் எல்வளை; the வ் is the glide after பிரிந்தென, and the word is இறைகேழ் (cf. Natrinai 167 இறை ஏர் எல் வளை), split at the wrong place.
135: line 2 repeats ainkurunuru:176 line 3 (ஐதுஅமைந்து அகன்ற அல்குல்).
